name: Flat iron / hair straightener

lead: A flat iron uses two heated plates to straighten curly or wavy hair, and can also add bends and loose waves. The payoff is a smooth, sleek, styled look that is visible immediately.

Heat lets hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex be reshaped while the hair is held straight; they can re-form when hair gets damp, so the effect is temporary. A lab study with an automated iron found that repeated ironing at 120 to 175 degrees Celsius straightened curly hair irreversibly. Safety research on the tools themselves concerns mainly burns.

paras: People work through dry hair in sections, clamping and gliding the plates from root to end, and often use a heat-protectant product beforehand. Results last until the next wash or until moisture and humidity restore the natural shape.

Overuse of heated tools can cause severe hair damage, and hot plates can cause contact burns, including in children. Large studies linking hair straightening to cancers or fibroids mostly concern chemical relaxers rather than heated irons.

angle.text: A flat iron straightens curls or adds waves, producing a sleeker styled look that is visible immediately and lasts until the next wash. Heat reshapes the bonds in the hair, and the article covers heat damage.

lead: A flat iron, also called a hair straightener, is a heated styling tool with two plates that clamp and glide along sections of hair to straighten or reshape them. People use it to smooth curly or wavy hair into a sleek, even finish, and also to add bends or loose waves [1]. Because the result is visible immediately and washes out, it is one of the most accessible ways to change how a head of hair frames the face.

According to Wikipedia, heat straightening works by breaking hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex, which can re-form when the hair is exposed to moisture, and overuse of heated tools can cause severe hair damage [1][2]. A laboratory study with an automated iron found that repeated ironing at temperatures from 120 to 175 degrees Celsius produced irreversible straightening in curly hair, with a role for silicone products in the process [3]. Other laboratory work has measured protein loss and cuticle changes in hair heated with a flat iron [4].
Published safety research on flat irons themselves concerns mainly burns; larger epidemiological studies of hair straightening concern chemical relaxers rather than heated irons [5][6][7].

paras: Most flat irons use ceramic plates; lower-priced models have a single ceramic coating and higher-priced ones use several layers or solid ceramic. Later electric and ceramic models added adjustable heat settings and different plate sizes [1]. Some models run on butane or batteries, and some have an automatic shut-off to reduce fire risk [1].

Hot combs were sold in Europe and America by the 1870s, and French hairdresser Marcel Grateau is credited in Wikipedia with introducing heated metal tools for styling hair in that decade [1][2]. Madam C. J. Walker (1867-1919) built a fortune selling hair and skin products to Black women, and Wikipedia describes her system as including the application of iron combs to the hair; her haircare business made her one of the best known entrepreneurs of her era [8]. The Hair straightening article says she popularised the straightening comb in the early 1900s without having invented it, and that salon visits became a social institution in Black culture [2].

A patent issued on 14 December 1909 to Isaac K. Shero for two flat irons heated and pressed together is described as the first hair straightener [1]. Wikipedia notes that some women in the 1960s used clothing irons on their hair [1]. Later electric and ceramic models added adjustable heat settings and different plate sizes, and a ceramic straightening brush was patented in 2013, with Sharon Rabi's DAFNI brand releasing the first one in 2015 [1].

Heat softens hair so that its hydrogen bonds can be reshaped while the hair is held straight. Experimental work with an automated iron controlled temperature, contact force and gliding speed and examined keratin changes after repeated cycles at 120-175 degrees Celsius, finding irreversible straightening of curly hair [3]. Wikipedia notes that moisture can restore the original shape of the hair when the bonds re-form [1].

Wikipedia's Hair straightening article groups methods into temporary and chemical. Temporary methods include hot combs, flat irons, blow dryers used with a comb or round brush, large rollers on damp hair and heated straightening brushes, as well as the Dominican blowout; the hair tends to revert on exposure to water or humidity [2]. Keratin or Brazilian treatments apply a keratin layer and then flat-iron the hair, with results lasting about six months according to the article, while Japanese thermal reconditioning uses a chemical to loosen bonds, heat to reshape and a neutraliser to set the change [2]. Relaxers use sodium hydroxide or calcium hydroxide [2].
Chemical methods act on disulfide bonds in the hair shaft and change existing hair but not new growth, whereas heat tools rely on hydrogen bonds that moisture can reset [2][1].

Flat irons are widely used to straighten and smooth hair, and the laboratory work above shows a measurable straightening effect with heat [3]. Wikipedia says heat protectants can reduce damage from excessive heat or frequent straightening, which can include split ends [2].

In appearance communities the tool is also used for waves or bends; one looksmax.org user shared a photo after using a wide flat iron to give his hair a slight wave, and a respondent said it looked better and suggested a loose perm instead, while the poster said the style made his hairline look less high [9].

A 2019 comparative study heated tresses of virgin hair from Caucasian and Asian donors with a flat iron and used thermogravimetry, FTIR spectroscopy, protein-loss assays and scanning electron microscopy. Water vapour was released between 25 and 170 degrees Celsius, other gases from about 200 degrees, and the denaturation temperature was 237 degrees; protein loss was greater for Asian hair, and electron microscopy showed visible cuticle damage. The authors stressed controlling temperature during heat treatment [4].

A separate 2019 study compared bleaching and dyeing, thioglycolate straightening, brushing and flat ironing, and UV radiation on straight, wavy, curly and Afro-ethnic hair, relating hair curliness to the type of damage; the abstract highlights bleaching as the most aggressive treatment and reports no results specific to flat ironing [10].

No clinical trial of heated flat irons was found. Related human research concerns chemical hair straighteners rather than heated plates: a 30-participant clinical study of chemical straightening and hair structure [7], and Sister Study cohort analyses of straightener and relaxer use in relation to cancers and fibroids [5][6]. Heat straightening has been examined in laboratory work [3][4] and in a forensic burn study [11].

The plates become hot enough to cause contact burns. A forensic study of two cases of children with second-degree burns from straightener plates used experiments on pig skin to characterize the injuries [11]. Other research has examined how heated straightening affects drug content measured in hair samples [12][13], and a building-air study measured siloxane emissions during hair care product use [14].

Epidemiological studies on hair straightening and cancer or uterine fibroid outcomes generally concern chemical straighteners and relaxers, not heated irons; they are sometimes discussed alongside flat irons. Both analyses used data from the Sister Study cohort [5][6]. A separate 30-patient study found that chemical straightening increased hair smoothness and shine while the hair structure was examined for damage [7].
